Why would a children's heart surgeon ask Ferrari for help?
At Great Ormond Street Hospital in London, a baby has just survived heart surgery.
The baby still has to move from the operating theatre to intensive care.
Every tube, wire and monitor is unplugged, moved and plugged back in, with several teams around one tiny bed.
In that rush, small details slip through.
Two of its doctors recognised that rush from a Formula One pit stop.
Except there, twenty mechanics change four tyres in seconds without getting in each other's way.
Ferrari's crew studied videos of the hospital's handovers and picked them apart.
The fix came straight from the pit lane: one leader runs the handover, like the lollipop man.
Everyone gets one job in a fixed order, and a checklist makes sure nothing is forgotten.
Technical errors dropped by forty-two percent, and missing information was almost cut in half.
A sport obsessed with saving tenths of a second taught doctors to protect their smallest patients.
So next time someone asks you...
